analysis.one_liner: Bars landlords from rejecting renters who pay with housing vouchers and penalizes neglected assisted housing.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced January 3, 2025 with one cosponsor, was referred to three House committees and has seen no further action, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Housing Act to make it illegal to refuse a renter because of where their money comes from, including Section 8 vouchers, Social Security, disability benefits, and child support. It would fine landlords $100,000 for deliberately letting a unit fall into disrepair so it loses federal housing assistance, and $100,000 for every 30 days a federally assisted apartment is deliberately left vacant. It would also expand HUD's complaint line, publish landlord complaints on a public website, fund tenant anti-harassment programs, and offer landlords a tax credit for maintaining low-income units if they fix complaints within 30 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who use Section 8 vouchers or receive Social Security, disability, or child-support income, who today can be turned away solely because of their payment source. Tenants in federally assisted multifamily buildings also gain complaint channels, posted notice of their rights, and new penalties against landlords who push them out through neglect or harassment.

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'source of income' as a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, covering housing vouchers, rental assistance, Social Security and SSI benefits, Railroad Retirement benefits, child and spousal support, and payments from trusts or relatives, so landlords could not refuse tenants for using these incomes.

Imposes a $100,000 civil penalty on owners who act with the intent to make a unit too run-down to qualify for HUD assistance, and lets affected tenants sue for $50,000 per violation plus actual damages and moving costs.

Penalizes owners of federally assisted multifamily projects $100,000 for every 30 days a unit is intentionally left vacant beyond 60 days, with repairs presumed legitimate unless a reasonable renovation period has clearly passed.

Requires HUD to staff the Multifamily Housing Complaint Line adequately, run a complaint resolution program with mediation, publish complaints on a public website with the building identified, report annually to Congress, and require posted tenant-rights notices in English and Spanish on every floor.

Authorizes $90 million a year for fair-housing enforcement grants, $47 million a year for state and local fair-housing agencies, $3 million a year for a public-awareness campaign, and $25 million a year for tenant harassment prevention programs offering legal help.

Gives landlords a tax credit equal to their maintenance costs on low-income units, capped at $500,000 per year, but only if they remedy any filed complaint within 30 days and keep rents at or below the federal fair-market level.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords of federally assisted rental housing, who would face penalties, public complaint disclosure, and vacancy limits; and taxpayers generally, who would fund roughly $165 million a year in authorized enforcement and grant spending plus a new landlord tax credit.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes large new federal spending, including $90 million plus $47 million annually for a decade for fair-housing enforcement, $25 million a year for harassment-prevention grants, and a maintenance tax credit worth up to $500,000 per landlord per year, all of which adds to federal costs.
Steep penalties and vacancy fines could make some landlords decide that accepting voucher tenants is not worth the risk, shrinking the supply of units available to the very renters the bill protects.

The tenant protections depend heavily on HUD carrying out new programs, staffing a complaint line, and publishing complaints on schedule, which the bill funds largely through unspecified 'such sums as may be necessary' appropriations rather than guaranteed money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provision, banning source-of-income discrimination, addresses a real barrier: a voucher is worthless if landlords can refuse it, which many do. The penalties for warehousing vacant assisted units and letting units decay to lose HUD eligibility target documented problems, and the maintenance tax credit is structured as a carrot tied to fixing complaints. The main honest concerns are cost, the risk that heavy penalties push landlords out of voucher programs, and the fact that much of the enforcement machinery depends on future appropriations. On balance the bill's benefits to low-income renters would likely outweigh its costs, but its design leaves real execution questions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 3, 2025 and sent to three House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote; Congress is still in session, so it could still move but has shown no signs of doing so.

narrative.text: Representative Nydia Velázquez introduced the bill on January 3, 2025, the first day of the 119th Congress.
It was referred to the Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees, with consideration to be split among them as the Speaker determined.
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Democrat, and no further legislative action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, landlords of federally assisted housing are better off because the bill has not advanced: none of the penalties, vacancy fines, or public complaint disclosures have taken effect, while voucher holders remain without a federal source-of-income protection.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no opposition is recorded; support so far consists of one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, with no Republican or bipartisan backing shown.

industries.industry: Landlords of federally assisted multifamily rental housing
industries.note: The bill would fine them $100,000 for deliberately disqualifying units from HUD assistance and for warehousing vacant assisted units, and would publish tenant complaints about their buildings. The same bill offers them a maintenance tax credit worth up to $500,000 a year, effectively paying them to keep assisted units in repair and keeping them in the voucher program, so its protections for tenants rest partly on a subsidy to the industry being regulated.

industries.industry: Fair-housing enforcement and tenant legal-aid organizations
industries.note: The bill authorizes $90 million a year for Fair Housing Initiatives Program groups, $47 million a year for state fair-housing agencies, and $25 million a year for tenant harassment prevention grants, most of which flows to nonprofits and local governments doing legal and counseling work for tenants.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no committee action, and jurisdiction split across three committees more than a year after introduction, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing, markup, or floor vote in this Congress. Comparable housing-rights bills that start this way typically die in committee when the two-year session ends.
